articles.title: Taxpayers’ burden
articles.content: IN challenging times, ordinary citizens and businesses may be called upon to shoulder higher tax burdens to meet the unavoidable costs of maintaining a sovereign state. But citizens should not be expected to bear the burden of costs that are largely avoidable. When debt servicing consumes 125 per cent of the FBR taxes retained by the federal government, 68.5pc of its total revenues, and nearly three times the defence budget, such an extraordinary burden demands closer scrutiny. Is our public debt being managed prudently and efficiently? In Pakistan, where a large proportion of the population comprises practising Muslims, many people prefer to keep their savings in bank accounts that pay no interest. As a result, nearly 40pc of all bank deposits are held in current accounts, on which banks pay no interest. This gives Pakistani banks access to an exceptionally cheap source of funds, which they invest in government securities at exorbitantly high returns. According to the State Bank of Pakistan, banks paid an average interest rate of just 5.53pc on their total deposits in September 2026, including current accounts that pay no interest. Yet, in October 2026, the government was borrowing through 12-month treasury bills at 12.79pc — a gross difference of 7.26 percentage points. Is our public debt being managed prudently and efficiently? A prudent borrower would certainly have sought to negotiate a much narrower margin, perhaps 1-2 percentage points. Yet our government continues to borrow at substantially higher rates, raising serious questions about the management of public debt. Ultimately, taxpayers are asked to bear the cost of such generosity. The burden falls on petrol and diesel consumers paying the Petroleum Development Levy, as well as investors paying effective income tax rates of 50-60pc. High returns on relatively low-risk government securities have encouraged banks to attract more low-cost deposits, particularly current accounts. By June 2026, these accounts held Rs15.3 trillion, nearly 40pc of total deposits, up from 37pc a year earlier. SBP confirms that the Rs3.67tn increase in deposits during the first half of 2026 came mainly from current accounts. While much of Pakistan’s productive economy has struggled, bank deposits have tripled from Rs13.35tn in December 2018 to nearly Rs41tn in September 2026. But where has this enormous pool of savings gone? Into new industries, businesses and jobs, or increasingly into high-yield government securities, earning banks substantial returns at taxpayers’ expense? According to SBP, commercial banks held Rs40.36tn in government securities in September 2026. Applying the prevailing gross interest-rate differential of 7.26 percentage points to these holdings gives an estimated annualised differential of approximately Rs2.93tn. If government borrowing rates were limited to 1-2 percentage points above banks’ average deposit cost, the estimated annualised gross savings could reach Rs2,100-2,500 billion, subject to debt maturities and repricing. Even part of these savings could ease the lives of millions of households and thousands of struggling entrepreneurs by reducing the Petroleum Development Levy, multiple taxes on energy bills, and high income tax rates on salaries and businesses. Such a policy would also reduce SBP’s annual interest earnings by approximately Rs118bn, which would be just a fraction of the overall savings. The government should introduce a law that limits the interest paid to commercial banks on government securities to a reasonable 1-2 percentage points above what banks pay their depositors on average. The implementation process should ensure that monetary policy, government borrowing operations and financial stability are not disrupted. In order to bring transparency into debt management operations, the law should require the Ministry of Finance and SBP to publish quarterly reports showing how much the government borrows from banks and other investors, the interest it pays, and the cost of funds to banks. These reports should also disclose how much the government actually saves through lower borrowing costs. The potential annual savings of Rs2,100-2,500bn, once realised, should be passed on to taxpayers and businesses that have long borne the burden of excessive taxation, rather than being absorbed by increased government expenditure. The priority should be to reduce the Petroleum Development Levy and General Sales Tax on electricity bills, thereby lowering fuel and transport costs, easing the cost of living and production, and reducing inflationary pressures. The government should also double the annual income-tax exemption threshold from Rs600,000 to Rs1.2 million, providing much-needed relief to salaried individuals and low-income taxpayers. The government should also restore the Final Tax Regime for exporters, making tax deducted from export proceeds their final income tax liability, even if the rate remains 2pc. This would simplify taxation, eliminate uncertainty and improve the competitiveness of Pakistani exporters by bringing their tax treatment closer to that of competitors in peer economies. Equally important is the complete abolition of the super tax, which reportedly generates around Rs400-500bn annually, but has become a major deterrent to new investment. The highest effective income tax rate on corporate, business and other incomes should be capped at 35pc, making Pakistan more attractive to investors while leaving greater disposable income available for savings, consumption and investment. Many such measures could be financed through the proposed annual debt-servicing savings of Rs2,100-2,500bn, provided the government pursues the necessary reforms with determination and ensures that the resulting fiscal space is used to reduce the tax burden rather than expand public expenditure. These measures would provide a much-needed stimulus to economic growth, encourage investment and job creation, and help alleviate poverty, which has become one of the country’s most pressing challenges. Reviving economic growth requires reducing the excessive tax burden on ordinary citizens and businesses — a burden that stifles investment, discourages enterprise and holds back economic activity. The writer is former federal finance secretary and currently chairman, Policy Research and Advisory Council.
articles.author: Mohammad Younus Dagha

articles.title: The IWT dilemma
articles.content: THE Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) of 1960 has long been heralded as one of the most durable water-sharing agreements in history. Despite multiple wars and decades of profound political animosity between India and Pakistan, the IWT managed to survive, providing a fragile framework for regulating the shared waters of the Indus River system. However, the delicate equilibrium of this treaty has been shattered. Themove by Indiato place the IWT in abeyance is not merely a diplomatic protest; it represents a fundamental strategic pivot. In an era increasingly defined by climate change and existential resource competition, the suspension of the IWT signals a shift toward a new, perilous world order where water security dictates state survival, and historical norms are rapidly eclipsed by the “law of the jungle.” To understand the severity of the hydro-political reality of scarcity, one must look beyond the immediate geopolitical friction and consider the changing hydrology and demography of the region. Climate change is rapidly altering the cryosphere of the Himalayas, which feeds the Indus basin. Glacial retreat, erratic monsoon patterns, and severe, prolonged droughts are making water availability increasingly unpredictable. The World Resources Institute (WRI) provides a stark warning in its Aqueduct Water Risk Atlas, mapping a future where water becomes the most prized — and contentious — resource on the planet. According to WRI projections, vast swathes of the globe, including South Asia, face escalating levels of baseline water stress. By mid-century, trillions of dollars in GDP will be exposed to high water risk as demand drasticallyoutstrips renewable supply. In such a landscape, water is no longer just an environmental issue; it is a fundamental driver of national security. As resources diminish, states are becoming increasingly inward-looking. The international order, which once placed a premium on cooperation, is giving way to a more ruthless framework where states prioritise their own existential needs above collective agreements. In this light, placing the IWT in abeyance is not a temporary diplomatic manoeuvre; it is a strategic preparation of the ground for an eventual unilateral withdrawal. As water scarcity increases, the temptation for an upper-riparian state to leverage control over water flows to secure its own agricultural and energy requirements becomes overwhelming, effectively treating the resource as sovereign property rather than a shared heritage. For Pakistan, the stakes are high because the Indus basin underpins agricultural production, rural livelihoods and food security. The intensification of India’s construction of storage dams along the Chenab River, despite the legal challenges and protests from Pakistan, is part of the strategic calculus and entirely consistent with this new paradigm. These projects allow for greater control, storage, and diversion of water. For Pakistan, an agrarian economy whose very existence relies on the Indus system, this is not a developmental disagreement — it is an existential threat. The Chenab-Beas link tunnel and the Salal sediment bypass illustrate the dilemma. Such projects may be presented as engineering responses to energy needs and sedimentation, yet transferring water between basins or modifying sediment-control infrastructure on a shared river raises both questions and concerns. The legal status and technical details of each project must be assessed individually for cumulative impact and downstream confidence. In August 2026 the Court of ArbitrationrejectedIndia’s unilateral abeyance of the treaty and reaffirmed that it remains in force. The court also ordered interim measures restricting specified construction at the Ratle hydroelectric project till 90 days after the Neutral Expert’s final decision expected in July 2027. India’s rejection of the court’s authority leaves a gap between legal pronouncement and practical compliance. The coming decision on pondage, spillways, low-level outlets and sediment flushing will matter, but the deeper question is whether both will accept a credible process for resolving disagreements. If the Neutral Expert and Court of Arbitration reach conflicting conclusions, and one or both governments dismiss the outcome, the treaty risks becoming an instrument that exists formally but no longer commands confidence. An institutional collapse would have consequences extending far beyond the immediate available water. It could erode hydrological data sharing, weaken flood warning cooperation, discourage investment in regional water management and intensify competition over reservoirs and infrastructure. A breakdown could also encourage unilateralism in transboundary river governance endangering peace at a time of growing geopolitical tensions and environmental fragility. The central danger remains the growing uncertainty in a system already under intense human pressure. For Pakistan, the stakes are high because the Indus basin underpins agricultural production, rural livelihoods and food security. For India, the consequences would include a more volatile neighbourhood, heightened diplomatic costs and a precedent that could complicate its own relations with other upstream countries. Neither country can insulate itself from the climatic and economic consequences of a destabilised basin. The gravity of the situation is exacerbated by the nuclear capabilities of both nations. The failure of the current global negotiations in limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius is also ensuring that hydrological instability will only worsen and add to the fear of scarcity. The international community must act before the legal impasse becomes a humanitarian and security crisis. Political wisdom and environmental diplomacy can also play a major role in averting a potential catastrophe. A nuclear-armed upstream power and a highly water-dependent nuclear-armed lower-riparian state cannot afford to let a river become an instrument of existential threat. If water insecurity contributes to political instability, military escalation or a wider regional confrontation, the consequences will not remain confined to South Asia.
articles.author: Aisha Khan

articles.title: Symbol of neglect
articles.content: NOTHING quite prepares you for the sensory overload you experience when you move from the pristine and polished Islamabad to the battered and potholed Karachi. To the discerning eye, Karachi looks like a low-resolution version of Islamabad, that too in sepia tones. The vibrancy of the “City of Lights” is mellowed by the haze of suspended smoke and dust, further muted by the drabness of its infrastructure. Its skyline, characterised by decrepit buildings woven through a not-so-intricate web of overhead wires, pales in comparison with Islamabad’s lush green, hilly landscape. The sounds of each city also stand in sharp contrast. While the latest and most luxurious private cars noiselessly cruise through Islamabad’s roads, Karachi’s streets are swarmed with motorbikes, rickshaws, buses, and trucks, each incessantly blaring its horn to force its way through traffic. Many private vehicles on the road bear visible signs of abuse inflicted by other heedless drivers. Both cities have their distinct olfactory signatures as well: while Islamabad exudes privilege and dewy freshness, Karachi reeks of injustice, neglect, and just pure garbage. The stench emanating from gutters, garbage sites, and at times, the sea is so overpowering that even the confines of an air-conditioned car fail to offer any respite from the pungency. Karachi’s disparity is unfortunate given its economic footprint. On the development front, as Islamabad witnesses the construction of new underpasses and bridges on a near-monthly basis, Karachi’s infrastructure crumbles under the weight of itsburgeoning population, exacerbated by the governance conundrum it faces. The city remains in shambles, ranking 170th out of 173 cities on theEIU’s Global Liveability Index 2026. This disparity is particularly unfortunate given Karachi’s enormous economic footprint, not to mention its remarkable capacity to embrace people from diverse backgrounds. The city accounts for nearly a quarter of Pakistan’s GDP, compared to Islamabad’s estimated 1-2 per cent. Yet, despite being nearly four times larger in area and having more than 10 times Islamabad’s population, Karachi receives a smaller share ofdevelopment allocations. Whatever resources are earmarked for the city are further fragmented between the Karachi Metropolitan Corporation (KMC) and provincial authorities, making coordinated urban development all the more difficult. The problem, however, extends far beyond the quantum of development spending. While several new development schemes have been announced for Karachi, those still enduring the (now) five-year-long nightmare ofconstruction along University Roadknow all too well that such projects bring far greater disruption than promise. Competing political interests, overlapping institutional mandates, and the persistent power struggle between provincial and local authorities undermine the effective and timely implementation of development projects. Karachi is not simply a poorly developed city; it is an economically indispensable one whose governance arrangements systematically undermine its capacity to convert economic activity into better urban outcomes. The political economy underpinning the disparity between the two cities is hardly difficult to discern. Unlike Islamabad, where the Capital Development Authority provides a relatively centralised structure for urban planning and development, Karachi is governed through a maze of overlapping jurisdictions, with municipal authorities, cantonment boards, development authorities, and provincial departments each vying for greater control. Competing interests and distorted mandates make it difficult to establish who is ultimately responsible for the city’s development, leaving its residents to bear the cost of institutional dysfunction. Moreover, a weak municipal revenue base and limited capacity for own-source revenue mobilisation leave local governments heavily dependent on provincial transfers, further entrenching their fiscal dependence and weakening their capacity to deliver urban services. It is deeply disheartening to see a city once synonymous with opportunity, enterprise, and the promise of a better life increasingly become a symbol of neglect, deprivation, and urban decay. Karachi needs more than sporadicdevelopment schemesand infrastructure projects. It needs empowered local governments, clearly defined institutional responsibilities, and predictable fiscal transfers that allow its elected representatives to plan and deliver services in line with the city’s needs. For a city that contributes so much to the country’s economy, the least it deserves is a governance system capable of delivering the most basic urban amenities. The writer is a development economist and policy consultant. She teaches economics at IBA, Karachi.
articles.author: Arooj Waheed Dar

articles.title: Sweeter than honey
articles.content: WE live in a world where tech giants like the frankly disturbing Peter Thiel rant about the antichrist and the excessively wealthy and extremely unlovable Elon Musk tries to foment racial discord via his own social media platform and names his children things like Tau Techno Mechanicus. What I’m saying is that things are weird, and getting weirder with every passing moment and so, it’s a relief to learn that (former) Nvidia CEOJensen Huangis at least a human being who succumbed not to the desire to turn himself into a cyborg but instead to the charms of a lady who may or may not be a Chinese spy out to milk him for critical tech-related information; the jury is still out on that but the verdict will come too late for Mr Huang. Nevertheless, if true, he fell for what is arguably one of the — if not the — oldest tricks in the book: the honeytrap. The first recorded mention of this classic gambit is in the Biblical story of Samson and Delilah. Samson, as the story goes, was a superhero of the ancient world whose great strength was the bane of his enemies. Naturally wanting to somehow weaken him by learning the source of his strength and negating it, his opponents found the beautiful and seductive Delilah who inveigled her way into his confidence and, having learned that the source of his strength was his long hair, proceeded to shave his head while he slept and thus allowed his enemies to capture him. But the real heyday of the honeytraps was during the world wars and then the Cold War. Here, I must caution those who may be thinking that falling for such a ploy is exclusively a male weakness. It’s not: Roald Dahl, the famous British author, apparently also served as a honeytrap whose mission was to win the hearts and minds of influential female writers, politicians and socialites in the United States so as to build a consensus in favour of the Allied war efforts. He was perfect for the job: a ‘skilled flirt’, standing at six foot six inches in his pilot’s uniform, oozing old-world charm and chock-full of wit, Dahl blazed a path through American high society in the early forties, famously seducing oil heiress Millicent Rogers and having an affair with Congresswoman Clare Booth Luce in an attempt to soften her views towards the British Empire. Success has its own drawbacks, and Dahl reportedly found the liaisons with the lawmaker so physically exhausting that he begged to be relieved of this duty only to be told to close his eyes and think of England. After all, much needs to be sacrificed for the greater national interest. The heyday of honeytraps was during the world wars & the Cold War. Dahl isn’t the only ‘Romeo spy’ on record as the East German Stasi — which ran one of the most pervasive intelligence networks to ever exist — operated an entire department of handsome and charismatic male spies to target lonely and vulnerable ‘Juliets’ who worked as assistants and secretaries in West German ministries, Nato offices, Western embassies and so on. It worked like a charm, providing the Eastern Bloc a steady stream of classified information. Honeytraps also need to be flexible enough to cater to any predilection, as the KGB demonstrated in the 1950s with British civil servant John Vassal, who was posted in the British embassy in Moscow. Quickly realising that Vassal was a repressed homosexual in an age where this practice was illegal in both Britain and the Soviet Union, they trapped him by using a Polish man to entice him into imbibing large amounts of alcohol at an ‘underground’ party for homosexuals in which he was photographed in compromising positions with a series of young men who had been trained precisely for this purpose. In fact, the entire party had been arranged by the KGB. With their hooks deep in him, the Soviets milked him for information that proved to be of the highest value to the Soviet defence chiefs in their successful drive to expand and modernise the Red Navy. The oddest honeytrap story of all time has to be the tale of French diplomat Bernard Boursicort, which has been immortalised in the play M. Butterfly, which was later turned into a film starring Jeremy Irons. Stationed in Beijing in the 60s, Boursicort began a 20-year affair with Chinese opera singer Shi Pei Pu who claimed to be a woman forced to dress like a man so that she could satisfy her father’s wish to have a son. In due course, while pressuring Boursicort into passing on several hundred secret documents and plying him with misinformation, she also produced a child that she claimed was the fruit of their liaisons. That was of course impossible because when they were finally arrested in 1983 it turned out that Pei had been a man all along. How did he then fool Boursicort for so long, given the intimate nature of their relationship? Well, you’ll just have to look that up yourself.
articles.author: Zarrar Khuhro

articles.title: LG malaise
articles.content: THE repeated delays in local government elections in Islamabad expose the reluctance of the government to strengthen democracy at the grassroots. The latest suspension by the IHC has again thrown the electoral process into uncertainty. The immediate dispute concerns the legal basis for delimitation. An ordinance issued in 2026 changed the capital’s LG structure. However, the ordinance lapsed, reviving the original 2015 law. The ECP proceeded with elections under the old law, even though the latest delimitation had been conducted under the new arrangement. This legal inconsistency has now stalled the electoral exercise. The problem goes beyond the latest dispute. Islamabad has been without an elected local government since February 2021. The ECP has conducted several delimitation exercises and announced multiple election schedules, but legislative changes and legal challenges have repeatedly disrupted the process. In a related development, the ECP has given the Prime Minister’s Office a fortnight to formally request elections in 42 cantonment boards. Their elected LGs completed their terms in April. But the centre has still not fulfilled the procedural requirements for fresh polls. These developments point to a deeper problem. Successive governments have shown little enthusiasm for devolving political and administrative authority to local representatives. LGs create independent centres of political power and accountability. Federal and provincial governments often appear more comfortable retaining control over local development funds and administrative decisions than allowing local bodies to decide their priorities. This reluctance carries a direct cost for citizens. LGs are best placed to identify neighbourhood needs and address problems that larger tiers of government often overlook. These problems cannot be resolved by distant government departments. They need elected representatives who remain answerable to residents. The importance of effective LGs becomes even greater during emergencies. Without functioning local institutions, even well-funded disaster responses often struggle to reach communities quickly. The constitutional requirement under Article 140-A to establish elected LGs reflects the importance of the third tier. Yet political commitments to devolution rarely translate into sustained institutional arrangements. Local bodies are allowed to function for limited periods before their terms expire, elections are delayed and administrative control returns to unelected officials. Electoral schedules should not remain hostage to indecision or repeated legislative changes. Residents deserve functioning local bodies that can address their everyday problems and respond when crises strike. Devolution must become a continuing democratic commitment rather than an arrangement governments honour only when convenient.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Smog diplomacy
articles.content: EACH winter, Lahore and Delhi engage in a peculiar rivalry, trading places at thetop of the world’s air-pollution rankings. On Friday, Delhi was declared the world’s most polluted major city while Lahore slipped to seventh. For people breathing this air, the distinction offers little comfort. A change in the weather can improve a city’s ranking without removing the sources of pollution. The smog that settles over northern India and Pakistan comes from vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions, dust and agricultural fires, compounded by winter conditions that trap pollutants near the ground. Much of this pollution is generated locally, and both governments have work to do at home. In Pakistan’s Punjab, satellites detected 18,825 fires, most believed to involve crop-residue burning. Lahore exceeded national standards for fine particulate matter on all 40 days covered by a recent assessment. Punjab’s authorities report more inspections, penalties and closures targeting polluting industries and brick kilns. Enforcement is necessary, but its effects must outlast the smog season. There is also a regional dimension that neither government can afford to ignore. Polluted air crosses the border regardless of the state of bilateral relations. That makes theforthcoming visitof Pakistan’s climate change minister to New Delhi especially pertinent. He is due to attend an SCO gathering on civilisational dialogue. Air pollution is not the meeting’s purpose, but the visit offers a rare opportunity to broach practical cooperation with Indian officials. At a minimum, the two states could work towards jointly sharing air-quality measurements, forecasts, timely public health warnings and satellite information on crop fires. Their scientists could jointly examine how pollution travels across the border. Such efforts need not await a broader diplomatic thaw. Nor should they provide either side with an excuse to blame its neighbour for pollution it has failed to control at home. The SCO already provides a channel through which officials from both countries meet, despite strained relations. The minister should use that opening to make the case for sustained regular technical contact on smog. With millions enduring another winter of dangerous air, even a modest conversation would be useful.
articles.author: Editorial
